title: A Replication of Karlan and List (2007)
text:
In the economics of charitable giving, a central question is whether the “price” of giving affects donor behavior. Dean Karlan and John List designed a natural field experiment to explore this by mailing over 50,000 donation solicitations to previous contributors of a politically liberal nonprofit. The solicitations randomly varied the presence and size of a matching grant — where a “leadership donor” promised to match contributions at ratios of $1:$1, $2:$1, or $3:$1 — to see how this influenced the likelihood and size of donations.
This intervention simulates a price change: for example, under a $2:$1 match, a $1 donation turns into $3 for the organization, lowering the “price” of public good provision from $1 to 33 cents. But does this lead people to give more?
This blog post replicates some of Karlan and List’s main findings using their publicly shared data. We aim to explore how the match offer affected donation behavior, whether larger match ratios increased giving, and what this implies about human motivation in philanthropic settings.

Description
The dataset used in this analysis was provided by Karlan and List as part of their 2007 publication. It contains 50,083 observations — one for each individual who received a fundraising letter during the experiment.
Each observation includes variables related to: - Treatment assignment: whether the individual received a matching offer and what kind. - Donor behavior: including whether they gave (gave) and how much (amount). - Experimental conditions: such as the matching ratio offered (ratio), the suggested donation (ask), and the match threshold (size). - Demographics and history: such as gender (female), number of prior donations (freq), and previous contribution size (hpa).
This dataset enables a detailed analysis of how price framing and appeal design influence charitable behavior in a real-world setting.

title: A Replication of Karlan and List (2007)
text:
Experimental Results
I conducted a balance check on mrm2 (months since last donation), a pre-treatment variable. Both a t-test and a bivariate regression confirm there is no statistically significant difference between treatment and control groups (p ≈ 0.905). This indicates that randomization was successful.
The coefficient from the regression is 0.014 (p = 0.905), meaning treatment and control groups differed by less than 1/50th of a month — an economically and statistically negligible amount.
Table 1 in Karlan & List (2007) serves a similar purpose: it demonstrates that observed covariates are balanced across groups, supporting the credibility of causal claims. Including such a table — and running our own check — assures readers that any observed treatment effects are not artifacts of selection bias.

This figure illustrates that the match treatment increased donation rates from 1.8% to 2.2%. While the change may seem small in absolute terms, it represents a 22% relative increase — which is substantial in a fundraising context.

The treatment group gave about $1.67 less than the control group, but this difference is not statistically significant (p ≈ 0.56). This suggests that matching offers do not affect how much people give, conditional on donating.
However, this regression does not have a causal interpretation, since we’re conditioning on a post-treatment variable (gave). Instead, it just describes the behavior of the subgroup of people who donated.

These plots confirm that donation size distributions are similar between groups, reinforcing the conclusion that matching grants influence whether people give — not how much they give once they do.

title: A Replication of Karlan and List (2007)
text:
Simulation Experiment
As a reminder of how the t-statistic “works,” in this section I use simulation to demonstrate the Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem.
Suppose the true distribution of respondents who do not get a charitable donation match is Bernoulli with probability p=0.018 that a donation is made.
Further suppose that the true distribution of respondents who do get a charitable donation match of any size is Bernoulli with probability p=0.022 that a donation is made.

Law of Large Numbers
To demonstrate how the sample average converges to the true treatment effect, I simulate donation behavior under the assumed probabilities (p=0.018 for control, p=0.022 for treatment):









This chart illustrates the Law of Large Numbers: although the early estimates are noisy, the cumulative average of simulated differences gradually stabilizes around the true effect of 0.004 as the sample size grows.


Central Limit Theorem
We simulate the average treatment effect at sample sizes of 50, 200, 500, and 1000. For each size, we run 1,000 simulations, where we take n random draws from both control and treatment distributions and compute the difference in means.









As the sample size increases, the histogram of simulated differences becomes narrower and more bell-shaped. This is a visual demonstration of the Central Limit Theorem, which shows why large sample sizes are critical for accurate statistical inference.

title: Poisson Regression Examples
text:
Blueprinty is a small firm that makes software for developing blueprints specifically for submitting patent applications to the US patent office. Their marketing team would like to make the claim that patent applicants using Blueprinty’s software are more successful in getting their patent applications approved. Ideal data to study such an effect might include the success rate of patent applications before using Blueprinty’s software and after using it. Unfortunately, such data is not available.
However, Blueprinty has collected data on 1,500 mature (non-startup) engineering firms. The data include each firm’s number of patents awarded over the last 5 years, regional location, age since incorporation, and whether or not the firm uses Blueprinty’s software. The marketing team would like to use this data to make the claim that firms using Blueprinty’s software are more successful in getting their patent applications approved.




import pandas as pd

blueprinty = pd.read_csv("/home/jovyan/Desktop/mysite/projects/hw2/blueprinty.csv")

blueprinty.info()
blueprinty.describe()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import seaborn as sns

sns.set(style="whitegrid")

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.histplot(data=blueprinty, x="patents", hue="iscustomer", bins=30, kde=False, multiple="dodge")
plt.title("Distribution of Patents by Customer Status")
plt.xlabel("Number of Patents")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.legend(title="Is Customer", labels=["Non-Customer", "Customer"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

blueprinty.groupby("iscustomer")["patents"].mean().round(2)

plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()

🧠 Observations The age distribution of customers and non-customers differs slightly. Boxplots indicate that customers tend to be slightly older, with a higher median age. This could reflect greater experience or longer time in the industry.
In terms of region, some areas show a stronger customer presence than others, suggesting regional variation in demand or outreach success. Understanding these patterns could help Blueprinty better target its services geographically.



Since our outcome variable of interest can only be small integer values per a set unit of time, we can use a Poisson density to model the number of patents awarded to each engineering firm over the last 5 years. We start by estimating a simple Poisson model via Maximum Likelihood.

Next, we extend our simple Poisson model to a Poisson Regression Model such that \(Y_i = \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)\) where \(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)\). The interpretation is that the success rate of patent awards is not constant across all firms (\(\lambda\)) but rather is a function of firm characteristics \(X_i\). Specifically, we will use the covariates age, age squared, region, and whether the firm is a customer of Blueprinty.

todo: If you’re feeling mathematical, take the first derivative of your likelihood or log-likelihood, set it equal to zero and solve for lambda. You will find lambda_mle is Ybar, which “feels right” because the mean of a Poisson distribution is lambda.
todo: Find the MLE by optimizing your likelihood function with optim() in R or sp.optimize() in Python.



Next, we extend our simple Poisson model to a Poisson Regression Model such that \(Y_i = \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)\) where \(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)\). The interpretation is that the success rate of patent awards is not constant across all firms (\(\lambda\)) but rather is a function of firm characteristics \(X_i\). Specifically, we will use the covariates age, age squared, region, and whether the firm is a customer of Blueprinty.
todo: Update your likelihood or log-likelihood function with an additional argument to take in a covariate matrix X. Also change the parameter of the model from lambda to the beta vector. In this model, lambda must be a positive number, so we choose the inverse link function g_inv() to be exp() so that \(\lambda_i = e^{X_i'\beta}\). For example:
poisson_regression_likelihood <- function(beta, Y, X){
   ...
}
todo: Use your function along with R’s optim() or Python’s sp.optimize() to find the MLE vector and the Hessian of the Poisson model with covariates. Specifically, the first column of X should be all 1’s to enable a constant term in the model, and the subsequent columns should be age, age squared, binary variables for all but one of the regions, and the binary customer variable. Use the Hessian to find standard errors of the beta parameter estimates and present a table of coefficients and standard errors.
todo: Check your results using R’s glm() function or Python sm.GLM() function.
todo: Interpret the results.
todo: What do you conclude about the effect of Blueprinty’s software on patent success? Because the beta coefficients are not directly interpretable, it may help to create two fake datasets: X_0 and X_1 where X_0 is the X data but with iscustomer=0 for every observation and X_1 is the X data but with iscustomer=1 for every observation. Then, use X_0 and your fitted model to get the vector of predicted number of patents (y_pred_0) for every firm in the dataset, and use X_1 to get Y_pred_1 for every firm. Then subtract y_pred_1 minus y_pred_0 and take the average of that vector of differences.

title: Poisson Regression Examples
text:
AirBnB Case Study

Introduction
AirBnB is a popular platform for booking short-term rentals. In March 2017, students Annika Awad, Evan Lebo, and Anna Linden scraped of 40,000 Airbnb listings from New York City. The data include the following variables:






Variable Definitions





- `id` = unique ID number for each unit
- `last_scraped` = date when information scraped
- `host_since` = date when host first listed the unit on Airbnb
- `days` = `last_scraped` - `host_since` = number of days the unit has been listed
- `room_type` = Entire home/apt., Private room, or Shared room
- `bathrooms` = number of bathrooms
- `bedrooms` = number of bedrooms
- `price` = price per night (dollars)
- `number_of_reviews` = number of reviews for the unit on Airbnb
- `review_scores_cleanliness` = a cleanliness score from reviews (1-10)
- `review_scores_location` = a "quality of location" score from reviews (1-10)
- `review_scores_value` = a "quality of value" score from reviews (1-10)
- `instant_bookable` = "t" if instantly bookable, "f" if not



todo: Assume the number of reviews is a good proxy for the number of bookings. Perform some exploratory data analysis to get a feel for the data, handle or drop observations with missing values on relevant variables, build one or more models (e.g., a poisson regression model for the number of bookings as proxied by the number of reviews), and interpret model coefficients to describe variation in the number of reviews as a function of the variables provided.
